unit.unitOverview: The last unit of the course. It maps Level 2, assembles it into three pieces of real work, and teaches one thing that is not in any other unit: how to decide what to learn next when nobody is telling you. Level 3 exists in the plan and not yet on the page, so from here you are your own syllabus — and that is a skill rather than a misfortune.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. It maps the level and adds one new thing.
Open Patterns. Card 1 is your map. Card 2 is what happens after this course.
Learn the words. Twenty, in four groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is two learners' plans for the year after.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is the diagnostic for the whole level.
Build the portfolio, record the presentation, write the plan.
Take the exit assessment, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
This is the last unit, so let me start with the map and then give you the one thing this course has not taught you yet.
Level 2 was about independence, and the name was accurate. Level 1 gave you the forms; this level gave you the judgements.
Units 1 to 5 built the machinery. Telling your story, describing precisely, the perfect aspect, relative clauses, conditionals. That is where your sentences stopped being short.
Units 6 to 12 were about connection and control. Joining ideas, disagreeing well, building words, reporting speech, the passive, narrating the past, verb patterns. Most of what makes writing sound adult rather than assembled is in those seven units.
Units 13 to 19 were about judgement. Certainty, applying for work, money and complaints, judging sources, hedging evidence, register, argument. Very little of that is grammar at all.
And that shift is the shape of the whole level. You began by learning what English can do and ended by learning what to do with it.
Now, if you revise anything, revise these six.
The present perfect and its contrast with the past simple, from Unit 3. It is the most-used thing in the level and the tense English speakers notice.
Relative clauses and the dropped pronoun, from Unit 4. It changes the length of your sentences more than anything else.
The conditionals, from Unit 5, and particularly the second — because if I were you is how English gives advice.
The comma splice, from Unit 6. It is the most common punctuation error in English and you can now avoid it.
The reporting verbs, from Unit 9, and the passive from Unit 10, because those two together are how English removes people from sentences, and you can now both do it deliberately and see it done.
And the warrant, from Unit 19. It is the newest idea in the level and the one that will change most arguments you have.
Now the new thing, and it is the only genuinely new content in this unit.
Level 1 Unit 19 taught you to find your own errors — record, listen twice, sort into what you know and what you do not. That still works and you should keep doing it.
This is the level above: deciding what to learn next.
Until now a course has decided that for you. From here, mostly nobody will, and the difference between people who continue improving and people who stop is almost entirely about this.
Here is what happens if you do not decide. You continue using English, you get more comfortable, and you improve for perhaps six months and then stop. That is the plateau, and it is not a failure of effort. It is what happens when you only ever practise what you already do — you become faster at your existing English and you do not acquire any more of it.
The way out has three parts.
First: find the gap, and find it from evidence rather than from feeling. Record yourself, as in Level 1. Look at what you avoid, not what you get wrong. The structures you never attempt are invisible in your output and they are where your ceiling is.
Second: choose one thing and set a deadline. Not five things. One structure, or one area of vocabulary, for a month. The failure mode here is a list of twelve things, all of which stay on the list.
Third — and this is the part that is genuinely different from being taught — build the practice yourself. Nobody is going to give you twelve exercises. What you do instead is force the structure into real use: decide that this week every email you write will contain a relative clause with a dropped pronoun, or that you will use the present perfect continuous in conversation three times. It feels artificial and it works, because the structure moves from something you understand to something you produce.
And there is a fourth thing which is not a step but a condition. You need input above your level. Reading and listening to English that is slightly too hard is where new structures come from, and no amount of practising what you have will substitute for it. Comfortable input maintains; difficult input builds.
One last honest thing, because this is the end of the course.
You are at B1. That means you can handle most everyday and work situations, follow the main points of clear speech, and produce connected text on familiar subjects. It also means that abstract discussion, fast conversation between other people, and reading anything written for a specialist audience are all still hard.
That is not a shortfall. It is what B1 is. Level 3 in this plan is B2, and the distance between them is roughly the same as the distance you have just covered — which should tell you both that it is a lot and that you have already done it once.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: What You Avoid, Not What You Get Wrong
readings.passageScript:
Level 1 Unit 19 taught you to find your errors: record two minutes, listen twice, sort what you find into things you know and things you do not.
That still works. This is the level above it, and it is about a different kind of gap.
Errors are visible. You said she work here, you hear it back, you fix it.
Avoidance is invisible. You wanted to say something and you went round it, and the recording contains no trace of what you meant to say — only the simpler thing you said instead.
And avoidance, not error, is what sets your ceiling.
A learner who makes eleven errors in two minutes while attempting complicated things is further ahead than one who makes none while attempting only what they are sure of. The second learner sounds better and will improve more slowly, because nothing is being stretched.
So the question at this level is not what did I get wrong. It is what did I not attempt.
There are three ways to find out, and none of them is comfortable.
Speak about something too difficult. Choose a subject you would struggle to explain in your first language — a decision that had competing reasons, a disagreement where both sides had a point. Simple topics let you use simple English and tell you nothing.
Write the same thing twice, once with a rule you must follow. Write a paragraph, then rewrite it with at least two relative clauses and one past perfect. If the second version says something the first could not, the first was avoiding.
And ask somebody. A person who knows both your English and the subject can often name what you are working around, because they can see the gap between what you clearly mean and what you actually said.
One finding is almost universal at this level and worth expecting. Most learners at B1 avoid the same three things: the perfect tenses, relative clauses with dropped pronouns, and anything that requires stating a position and then qualifying it. All three are in this level. Knowing which you avoid is the beginning of the plan.

readings.title: The Plateau Is a Failure of Input
readings.passageScript:
Here is what happens to most people who finish a course and keep using the language.
They improve for about six months. Then they stop, and they continue not improving for years, while using English every day and feeling that they should be getting better.
That is the plateau, and it is not a failure of effort or of talent. It is what happens when all your practice is at your own level.
Using English that you already have makes you faster and more comfortable at it. It does not give you any more of it. The structures you do not have cannot be discovered by using the ones you do.
So the way off the plateau has one non-negotiable condition and three steps.
The condition is input above your level. Reading and listening to English that is slightly too hard is where new structures come from, and nothing else supplies them. Comfortable input maintains. Difficult input builds. If everything you read is easy, you will not plateau in six months — you are on the plateau now.
Slightly too hard is the calibration that matters. Material where you understand most of it and have to work for the rest. If you understand everything, it is too easy. If you understand a quarter, you are decoding rather than reading and you will stop.
Then the three steps.
Find one gap, from evidence. Not from a feeling that your grammar is bad — from a recording, a rewrite, or somebody who told you.
Choose one thing and set a date. One structure or one area, for four weeks. Twelve things on a list is the commonest failure, and it fails because nothing on a list of twelve is ever the thing you do today.
Build the practice yourself. This is what is different about learning without a course: nobody hands you exercises. You force the structure into real use — this week every email contains a relative clause with a dropped pronoun, or I use the past perfect three times in conversation. It feels artificial and it works, because it moves a structure from understood to produced, which is the only transition that matters.
And keep the benchmark. Record two minutes now and put it somewhere. In six months you will not be able to hear your own progress, because you are inside it. The recording will.

PLAN A

  Goals for next year:

  - Improve my grammar generally
  - Learn more vocabulary
  - Get better at speaking
  - Read more
  - Watch films in English
  - Improve pronunciation
  - Work on my writing
  - Maybe take an exam

  I will study for one hour every day and
  review everything from both levels. I
  want to be fluent by the end of the
  year.

-----------------------------------------

  PLAN B

  Benchmark: 2-minute recording made
  today, on why I left my last job.
  Kept in the same folder as this.

  What I avoid (from that recording):
  the past perfect - twice I said \"before
  that I worked\" where I meant \"I had
  worked\"; and I never once qualified a
  claim, so everything came out flatter
  than I meant it.

  One target, four weeks: the past perfect
  in speech.

  Practice I will actually do:
  - Tuesday and Thursday, 10 minutes:
    describe something that happened,
    out of order, out loud.
  - Every work email that mentions a
    sequence: one past perfect.

  Difficult input: one podcast episode a
  week where I understand about 70 per
  cent. Not the news - I already follow
  that comfortably.

  Check: re-record the same two minutes
  on 20 May and count.

  If a week goes badly I do the Tuesday
  ten minutes and nothing else. That is
  the minimum, not the target.

grammar.explanation: The only new content in this unit, and the most important. Level 1 Unit 19 taught you to find your errors. This is how you decide what to learn when nobody is deciding for you.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE CONDITION (not a step)
  INPUT ABOVE YOUR LEVEL.
  Comfortable input MAINTAINS.
  Difficult input BUILDS.

  "slightly too hard" = you understand
  MOST and work for the rest.
     all of it -> too easy
     a quarter -> decoding; you stop

THE THREE STEPS

  1 FIND ONE GAP, FROM EVIDENCE
     a recording, a forced rewrite, or
     somebody who told you.
     Look for what you AVOID, not what
     you get wrong.

  2 ONE THING, WITH A DATE
     one structure, four weeks.
     A list of twelve fails - nothing on
     it is ever today's job.

  3 BUILD THE PRACTICE YOURSELF
     force it into real use:
       every email this week contains X
     Artificial, and it works - it moves
     a structure from UNDERSTOOD to
     PRODUCED.

  record two minutes now. In six months
  you cannot hear your own progress.
grammar.workedExample:
You have finished the course and want to keep improving.
1. Record two minutes on something genuinely difficult — a decision with competing reasons, not your daily routine. Keep it; it is your benchmark.
2. Listen twice, as in Level 1 Unit 19. Then ask the new question: what did I want to say and go round?
3. Suppose you find that you twice said before that I worked where you meant I had worked, and that you never once qualified a claim.
4. Choose one. The past perfect, for four weeks. Not both, and not the eight other things you know are weak.
5. Now build practice, because nobody will give you any. Two ten-minute sessions a week describing something out of order, aloud. And a rule for real use: every work email mentioning a sequence gets one past perfect.
6. Set the condition: one podcast episode a week where you understand about seventy per cent. Not the one you already follow comfortably.
7. Set a date to re-record the same two minutes and count.
8. And set a minimum — what you do in a week that goes badly. Ten minutes on Tuesday and nothing else.
That last step is what makes it survive a difficult month, and it is the one people leave out.
grammar.commonMistake: Making a list of everything you want to improve. Twelve goals is not a plan, because nothing on a list of twelve is ever the thing you do today, and a month later all twelve are still on it. The other error is practising only what is comfortable — using English you already have makes you faster at it and gives you no more of it, which is exactly what the plateau is.

writing.promptAndInstructions:

1. Unit 4, the plain-English rewrite of clause 7.3. Shows: relative clauses, and knowing when to split a sentence instead. Now: I would number the conditions rather than listing them in prose.
2. Unit 9, the two reports of one statement. Shows: reported speech, and that the reporting verb carries a judgement. Now: my Report B is too obviously loaded — real ones are subtler than that.
3. Unit 15, the complaint. Shows: five parts, a named remedy and a date. Now: my remedy is still slightly vague — I asked for it to be replaced without saying by when.

5. Unit 18, the same request at three levels. Shows: register control. Now: my middle version drifted too close to the formal one.
6. Unit 19, the full argument. Shows: claim, evidence, warrant and a real rebuttal. Now: my caveat is at the end where it is easy to skip.

COVERING STATEMENT
At the start of this level I could describe things and follow instructions. I could not argue, and I could not tell the difference between a fact and a judgement in something I was reading.
Now I can build a case with evidence, state what I am assuming, and answer the strongest version of the other side. I can read a report and see where certainty was added. I can move between registers deliberately rather than by accident.
My main strength is a habit rather than a skill: I state my warrant when an argument sticks, and it has ended two disagreements at work that had been going for months.
My main weakness is the past perfect in speech. I have it in writing and I go round it when talking, using the past simple twice where the order was not obvious.

writing.promptAndInstructions:

BENCHMARK Two-minute recording made today on why I changed jobs. Saved in the same folder as this file, dated.

THE GAP From that recording: I used the past simple twice where the order needed the past perfect — before that I worked there for I had worked there. I also never qualified a single claim in two minutes, so everything came out flatter and more certain than I meant.

- Tuesday and Thursday, ten minutes: describe something that happened, out of order, aloud, recorded.
- Every work email mentioning a sequence: one past perfect. Roughly three a week.

1. I am least confident about the podcast. Seventy per cent is uncomfortable and my instinct will be to go back to something easier, which would put me straight back on the plateau.
2. The plan would stop entirely if I dropped the Tuesday session for two consecutive weeks. That is the point at which momentum goes, so if it happens I restart at five minutes rather than abandoning it.

1. Plan B. Plan A's eight goals are all vague and none of them can be started on a particular morning, so in three months all eight will still be there. No key — it is your recording. But three findings are close to universal.
The error list is shorter than expected and the avoidance list is longer. Errors feel like the problem and they are usually the smaller half.
At least one of the three named structures will be entirely absent from two minutes of difficult speech. Absent, not wrong — you will find zero relative clauses with dropped pronouns, or zero perfect tenses, in a passage where several would have been natural.

Most learners at this level state positions flatly, not because they are certain but because hedging requires an extra clause and the sentence is already hard. activities.instructionsAndItems:
Find three sources of English that are slightly too hard — one to read, one to listen to, one either.
For each, test the calibration: do you understand most of it and have to work for the rest?
If you understand everything, it is too easy. If you understand a quarter, it is too hard and you will stop.

No key.
